lessons.title: First steps at an emergency
lessons.html:
The first aider's job

First aid is the help you give an injured or sick person until a nurse, paramedic or doctor takes over. Good first aid can save a life, stop an injury getting worse and help the person recover. This lesson is not enough to make you a first aider. You must do hands-on training and assessment with an accredited first aid training provider. The OHS Act 85 of 1993 requires employers to provide first aid boxes and trained first aiders at work.

Remember DRSABC

  1. D - Danger: check for danger to you, bystanders and the person. Switch off machines, turn off electricity, keep away from animals, traffic, fire or chemicals. Do not become a second casualty.
  2. R - Response: tap the shoulders and shout: "Can you hear me? Open your eyes." If there is no response, the person is unconscious.
  3. S - Send for help: shout for help. Ask someone to call an ambulance (10177, or 112 from a cell phone) and to bring the first aid box and an AED (defibrillator) if there is one.
  4. A - Airway: tilt the head back gently and lift the chin to open the airway.
  5. B - Breathing: look, listen and feel for normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds.
  6. C - CPR: if the person is not breathing normally, start CPR.

Protect yourself

  • Wear disposable gloves from the first aid box when touching blood or body fluids.
  • Use a face shield or pocket mask for rescue breaths if you have one.
  • Wash your hands well afterwards.

When the person is breathing

If an unconscious person is breathing normally and you do not suspect a spinal injury, put them in the recovery position: on their side, top leg bent, head tilted back so that vomit can drain out. Keep checking their breathing until help arrives.

lessons.title: CPR, choking and bleeding
lessons.html:
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) for adults

  1. Kneel next to the person, who must be on their back on a firm surface.
  2. Put the heel of one hand in the centre of the chest, the other hand on top, fingers locked.
  3. With straight arms, push down hard about 5 to 6 cm, then let the chest come back up.
  4. Push fast: 100 to 120 compressions a minute.
  5. After 30 compressions, give 2 rescue breaths if you are trained and willing. If not, keep doing chest compressions only.
  6. Continue 30 compressions to 2 breaths until help arrives, an AED is ready, the person starts breathing normally, or you are too tired to go on.
  7. If an AED arrives, switch it on and follow its voice instructions.

Choking (adult who cannot breathe, cough or speak)

  1. Ask: "Are you choking?" If they can cough, encourage them to keep coughing.
  2. If they cannot cough, lean them forward and give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades.
  3. If that does not work, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts: stand behind them, fist above the navel, pull sharply in and up.
  4. Repeat 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts. If they become unconscious, call for help and start CPR.

Severe bleeding

  • Put on gloves.
  • Press firmly on the wound with a clean pad or dressing.
  • Keep pressing. If blood soaks through, add another pad on top; do not remove the first one.
  • Bandage the pad firmly in place.
  • Lay the person down and keep them warm. Get medical help.
  • If an object is stuck in the wound, do not pull it out. Press around it.

lessons.title: Burns, shock, fractures and farm emergencies
lessons.html:
Burns

  • Cool the burn under cool running water for about 20 minutes.
  • Remove rings and watches before swelling starts, but do not pull off clothing stuck to the burn.
  • Cover loosely with cling wrap or a clean, non-fluffy dressing.
  • Never put butter, oil, toothpaste or ice on a burn. Do not burst blisters.
  • For chemical burns, rinse with plenty of running water and check the product label or safety data sheet.

Shock

Shock is a life-threatening condition after severe bleeding, burns or other injuries. Signs: pale, cold, sweaty skin, fast weak pulse, fast breathing, confusion.

  • Lay the person down and raise the legs if this does not cause pain or harm.
  • Keep them warm with a blanket.
  • Do not give anything to eat or drink.
  • Get medical help urgently.

Fractures and sprains

  • Do not move the person unless they are in danger.
  • Support the injured part in the position you found it; use padding and a sling or splint if trained.
  • If you suspect a head, neck or back injury, keep the head still and wait for paramedics.

Farm and work emergencies

  • Snakebite: keep the person calm and still, remove rings, keep the bitten limb still and get them to hospital fast. Do not cut, suck, apply ice or use a tight tourniquet.
  • Chemical poisoning: remove from the source, remove contaminated clothing, rinse skin, and take the label to the hospital.
  • Eye splash: rinse with clean running water for a long time.

Always report the incident to your supervisor and write it in the incident register. Restock the first aid box after use.

Key points

  • Follow DRSABC: Danger, Response, Send for help, Airway, Breathing, CPR.
  • Adult CPR: 30 compressions (5 to 6 cm, 100 to 120 a minute) to 2 breaths, or compressions only.
  • Stop severe bleeding with firm direct pressure.
  • Cool burns under running water for about 20 minutes; never use butter or oil.
  • Hands-on training by an accredited first aid provider is required.
